learningObjectives.title: Levels of organisation and interdependence in ecosystems
Cycling of materials: carbon and water cycles and decomposition

questions.q: Which statement best defines an ecosystem?
options: The interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment
All the organisms of a single species living in one area
Only the living organisms found in a particular habitat
The physical conditions of a habitat considered on their own
questions.explain: An ecosystem includes both the biotic community and the abiotic environment and how they interact.

questions.q: What does the term 'population' mean in ecology?
options: All the organisms of a single species living in a habitat
All the different species living together in a habitat
All the living and non-living components of an area
The place where a particular organism lives
questions.explain: A population is all the members of one species in a given area at a given time.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a community?
options: All the populations of different species living in the same area
All the members of one species in a habitat
The abiotic factors acting on organisms
A single organism interacting with its surroundings
questions.explain: A community is made up of all the interacting populations of different species in an ecosystem.

questions.q: Which of the following is an abiotic factor?
options: Light intensity
Availability of food
Presence of predators
Competition between plants
questions.explain: Abiotic factors are non-living conditions such as light, temperature, moisture and pH.

questions.q: Which of the following is a biotic factor?
options: The number of predators in the habitat
The soil moisture level
The air temperature
The intensity of light
questions.explain: Biotic factors are living influences such as predation, competition, food availability and disease.

questions.q: Two red deer stags competing for the same mates in a forest is an example of what?
options: Intraspecific competition
Interspecific competition
Mutualism
Predation
questions.explain: Intraspecific competition occurs between organisms of the same species for the same resources.

questions.q: Why are organisms in a community described as interdependent?
options: They rely on one another for resources such as food, shelter and pollination
They all belong to the same species
They never compete for any resources
They live in completely separate habitats
questions.explain: Interdependence means a change in one population can affect others that depend on it.

questions.q: In a food web, the number of rabbits falls sharply after a disease outbreak. What is the most likely immediate effect on the foxes that eat them?
options: The fox population is likely to fall due to less available food
The fox population will immediately rise
The foxes will be completely unaffected
The foxes will change into a new species
questions.explain: Removing a food source reduces the predator population that depends on it, showing interdependence.

questions.q: Which two processes return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
options: Respiration and combustion
Photosynthesis and respiration
Photosynthesis and combustion
Transpiration and condensation
questions.explain: Respiration by living organisms and combustion of fuels both release carbon dioxide into the air.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
options: Photosynthesis
Respiration
Combustion
Decomposition
questions.explain: Plants and algae take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to make glucose.

questions.q: What is the main role of microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi in the cycling of materials?
options: They decompose dead organisms, returning nutrients to the environment
They produce oxygen through photosynthesis
They prevent carbon from entering the soil
They convert light energy into food for plants
questions.explain: Decomposers break down dead matter and waste, recycling carbon and mineral nutrients.

questions.q: Which set of conditions would generally give the fastest rate of decomposition?
options: Warm, moist and well-oxygenated
Cold, dry and airless
Cold, moist and airless
Warm, dry and airless
questions.explain: Warmth, moisture and oxygen increase the activity of aerobic decomposers, speeding decay.

questions.q: In the water cycle, what is the name of the process by which water vapour turns back into liquid water?
options: Condensation
Evaporation
Precipitation
Transpiration
questions.explain: Water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds before falling as precipitation.

questions.q: Why is the cycling of materials such as carbon important for ecosystems?
options: It ensures elements are recycled so they can be reused by living organisms
It permanently removes carbon from living systems
It stops plants from photosynthesising
It prevents any energy transfer between organisms
questions.explain: Materials are finite, so cycling continually returns nutrients for reuse by future generations.

questions.q: What does the term 'biodiversity' refer to?
options: The variety of different species of organisms in an ecosystem
The total number of one species in a habitat
The non-living conditions of a habitat
The rate of decomposition in soil
questions.explain: Biodiversity is the range of different species within an ecosystem or on Earth.

questions.q: Why is high biodiversity generally beneficial to an ecosystem?
options: It makes the ecosystem more stable and less dependent on any single species
It guarantees every species will become extinct more slowly than expected
It reduces the number of food chains to just one
It removes all competition between organisms
questions.explain: Greater biodiversity provides more interdependent relationships, improving stability and resilience.

questions.q: Which human activity is most likely to reduce biodiversity?
options: Deforestation to create farmland
Planting a wide variety of native trees
Creating protected nature reserves
Rewilding an area of former farmland
questions.explain: Deforestation destroys habitats and reduces the variety of species an area can support.

questions.q: In a food chain, what name is given to organisms such as plants that make their own food by photosynthesis?
options: Producers
Primary consumers
Decomposers
Secondary consumers
questions.explain: Producers convert light energy into chemical energy and form the start of food chains.

questions.q: A student uses a 0.25 m2 quadrat and records a mean of 6 daisies per quadrat on a field. Estimate the total number of daisies in a 200 m2 field.
questions.explain: Estimated number = mean density x area = (6 / 0.25) x 200 = 24 x 200 = 4800.

questions.q: A student wants to investigate how the distribution of a plant changes from the edge of a wood into an open field. Which sampling method is most appropriate?
options: Placing quadrats at regular intervals along a transect line
Throwing quadrats randomly across the whole area
Counting every single plant in both habitats
Using a pooter to collect the plants
questions.explain: A belt transect with quadrats at set intervals shows how distribution changes along an environmental gradient.
